prompt: Two runners start side by side at $t = 0$ and run along the same straight track. Their velocities, in meters per second, are $v_A(t) = 2t + 1$ and $v_B(t) = t^2$ for $0 \le t \le 3$. How far ahead of runner B is runner A at $t = 3$ seconds, in meters?
hint: Each runner's distance is the integral of their velocity. The gap between them is the integral of the DIFFERENCE of velocities — the area between the two velocity curves.

hints.text: Each runner's distance is the integral of their velocity. The gap between them is the integral of the DIFFERENCE of velocities — the area between the two velocity curves.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: runner A covers $\int_0^3 (2t + 1) \, dt = [t^2 + t]_0^3 = 12$ m. Runner B covers $\int_0^3 t^2 \, dt = 9$ m.
Gap $= 12 - 9$, or directly $\int_0^3 (2t + 1 - t^2) \, dt = \left[t^2 + t - \frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^3$.

explanation: Position of each runner at $t = 3$: $s_A = \int_0^3 (2t + 1) \, dt = 9 + 3 = 12$ m and $s_B = \int_0^3 t^2 \, dt = 9$ m.
Equivalently, the gap is $\int_0^3 (v_A - v_B) \, dt = \int_0^3 (2t + 1 - t^2) \, dt = \left[t^2 + t - \frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = 9 + 3 - 9$.
$= 3$ m: A leads by $3$ meters. Note that $v_B > v_A$ once $t > 1 + \sqrt{2} \approx 2.41$, so B is already closing the gap by $t = 3$ — the signed area handles that automatically.

alternativeExplanations.title: Reading the graph
steps: Plot both velocity curves. From $t = 0$ to about $2.41$, the line $2t + 1$ is above the parabola $t^2$: A pulls ahead by that area.
From $2.41$ to $3$ the parabola is on top: B gains back that (smaller) area.
Net area $= 3$: A is still $3$ m ahead at $t = 3$, but B will catch up soon after.
